title: Drifting Field Policy: A One-Step Generative Policy via Wasserstein Gradient Flow
claim: Our method matches or beats strong baselines across many manipulation tasks, especially in the harder online fine-tuning settings.
layout: 12 panels in 4x3 grid, shared legend at bottom, gray offline phase shading
description: A 4x3 grid of line plots. Each plot shows success rate (0 to 1) against training steps (0 to 2×10^6). Panel titles run from Robomimic-lift, square and can through Cube-double, Cube-triple and Cube-quad tasks. The left half of each plot has a gray background for the offline phase, and the right half is white for the online phase. Six methods appear as colored lines with markers and shaded 95% confidence bands: BFN (purple), QC-BFN (light blue), FQL (gray), QC-FQL (orange), MVP (pink) and DFP (Ours) in dark navy. A shared legend sits at the bottom. The navy DFP curve usually rises sharply at the phase switch and ends at or near the top. It does best on the harder cube-triple and cube-quad tasks. Baselines like BFN and FQL often stay low.
caption: Success rate over training steps across Robomimic [ref] and OGBench [ref]. Solid lines and shaded regions show the mean and 95% confidence interval over five runs. Gray and white backgrounds indicate the offline and online phases, respectively.
abstract: We propose Drifting Field Policy (DFP), a non-ODE one-step generative policy built on the drifting model paradigm. We frame the policy update as a reverse-KL Wasserstein-2 gradient flow toward a soft target policy, so that each DFP update corresponds to a gradient step in probability space. By construction, this gradient is decomposed into an ascent toward higher action-value regions and a score matching with the anchor policy as a trust region. We further derive a simple, tractable surrogate of the otherwise intractable update loss, akin to behavior cloning on top-K critic-selected actions. We find empirically that this mechanism uniquely benefits the drifting backbone owing to its non-ODE parameterization. With one-step inference, DFP achieves state-of-the-art performance on several manipulation tasks across Robomimic and OGBench, outperforming ODE-based policies.
